description: a team hopelessly addicted to space, pixels, and questionable mission planning. We're channeling that addiction into a 2D pixel-art game where you design (and probably crash) your own space missions.
summary:
Margin is a 2D pixel-art platformer, made in Godot, that teaches children aged 7 to 12 how astronauts survive. The player is Max, a young astronaut who lands on Mars. A solar radiation storm forces him into a lava tube cave with no breathable air.

To get through, players share a small suit battery between Air, Shield and Light. Every cell given to one system is taken from another, so each choice has a cost. Power stations add new cells and forecast the area ahead, so kids plan the way real mission planners balance power, oxygen and radiation protection.

The danger comes from real NASA data. At startup, the game checks NASA's DONKI database for recent solar particle storms. If none happened, it uses a real stored storm and says so. Hidden scrolls unlock short, kid-friendly science chapters with their NASA sources, such as Curiosity's radiation readings and astronaut oxygen needs.

This matters because space science often feels distant to children. Margin turns it into decisions they make with their own hands, where failing is gentle and trying a new plan is part of the fun.
details:
What it does and how it works

Margin is a 2D pixel-art platformer about surviving on Mars. The player is Max, a young astronaut who has just landed. A solar radiation storm hits, and Max must shelter in a lava tube cave with no breathable air, full of lava pits, crumbling platforms, a radiation skylight and dark tunnels.

The core mechanic is a suit power budget. The suit starts with 3 battery cells, shared between three systems:

- Air: more cells make oxygen last longer.

- Shield: more cells make radiation build up more slowly.

- Light: more cells give a bigger headlamp, so you can see dangers and find secret paths.

Every cell given to one system is taken from another. Each Power Station adds one new cell, shows a forecast of the next area, and lets the player re-plan, the way real mission planners balance limited power.

Real NASA data drives the danger. When the game starts, it asks NASA's DONKI database for solar particle storms from the last 30 days. A strong real storm makes radiation build faster. If the Sun was quiet or the device is offline, the game uses one of 16 real storms measured by GOES satellites, and it always says which case applies. Three hidden scrolls unlock chapters in an in-game Book of Books, with kid-friendly science and NASA sources.

Benefits

- Children learn by doing: they feel the trade-off between air, radiation and light instead of reading about it.

- Every run uses a real storm, so the same plan can work one time and fail the next. That teaches kids to check conditions before acting.

- Failure is gentle. Max respawns nearby with air left, so experimenting is encouraged.

- Every fact in the game shows its source, and a NASA Data screen separates real science from game invention.

Intended impact

We want children to come away understanding that astronaut survival is about planning and trade-offs, and to become curious about real space science and NASA data. The game can be played alone, or used in a classroom where students compare the power plans they chose and how those plans turned out.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

- Game engine: Godot 4.7, programmed in GDScript.

- Art and sound: our own Python 3 scripts (using Pillow and NumPy) that generate the pixel art, tilesets, characters, portraits, logo and sound effects.

- Data: NASA DONKI API (api.nasa.gov) and NASA CCMC.

- Fonts: Silkscreen and Pixelify Sans (Open Font License).

- Version control: Git and GitHub.

- AI assistance: Claude Code, as described in our AI disclosure.

- Builds: exported for Windows, Linux and the web browser. Developed on desktop PCs; played with a keyboard.

How it is creative

Margin mixes a tight, fast platformer, inspired by games like Celeste, with a strategy layer about resource planning. Live space weather from NASA changes each run, so real events on the Sun change the game. The story adds humour through OG, a rude old wizard who laughs at Max. The main menu shows the MARGIN title over an animated Martian dust storm. Collectible scrolls reward exploration with real science instead of points.

Factors our team considered

- Age 7 to 12: short dialogue, big readable pixel text, and only three resources named in plain words.

- Honesty: stored data is never shown as live, every fact cites its source, and game fiction (like hot lava in a cold Martian lava tube) is labelled as fiction.

- Reliability: the game still works offline or when NASA's shared API key hits its request limit, by using real stored storms.

- Fun first: values are tuned for play, but every effect works in the same direction as real life.

- Replayability: different storms, secrets to find, and different power plans to try.

- No NASA logos or mission insignia in the artwork.
